# submission name:
hnerv_lc_ac

# upload zipped `archive.zip`
[archive.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27355831/archive.zip)

# report.txt
```
=== Evaluation results over 600 samples ===
  Average PoseNet Distortion: 0.00003443
  Average SegNet Distortion: 0.00057638
  Submission file size: 178,223 bytes
  Original uncompressed size: 37,545,489 bytes
  Compression Rate: 0.00474686
  Final score: 100*segnet_dist + √(10*posenet_dist) + 25*rate = 0.19
```

# does your submission require gpu for evaluation (inflation)?
no

# did you include the compression script? and want it to be merged?
no

# additional comments
This submission is a derivative of #95, so credit goes to @AaronLeslie138. Added a few tricks to push down the score to 0.19487 locally

Lossless byte-level repack of @BradyMeighan's `hnerv_lc_v2` (#100). Decoder weights, latents, and latent-correction sidecar are all his (built on @EthanYangTW's #98).

The substantive change: arithmetic coding (constriction range coder) on the 8 largest weight tensors and the latent-hi byte stream. Brady's pipeline uses pure brotli; switching the densest payloads to AC with q8 (uint8) histograms beats brotli's symbol-level entropy by ~290 B. Rest of the bytes come from hardcoded section lengths inside `inflate.py` (no length prefixes inside the archive), adaptive `lgwin` search in brotli, a single-byte filename inside the zip, and merging all 9 AC streams into one constriction `RangeEncoder` to eliminate per-stream rounding overhead.

@YassineYousfi could you re-run on CPU since my submission does not require GPU? The score has changed drastically from my observed 0.19847. Curious if that will drop it back down. Same for #96

I saw your reply in #95, but it's not "fair" to run these on GPU considering it will negatively affect some implementations but not all. Your required report has an explicit question on if GPU is required, and the rules state:

> The official evaluation has a time limit of 30 minutes. If your inflation script requires a GPU, it will run on a T4 GPU instance (RAM: 26GB, VRAM: 16GB), _**if it doesn't it will run on a CPU instance (CPU: 4, RAM: 16GB).**_

Thanks

you're welcome to run the workflow on your own fork. I think it's fair to run all submissions on the same hw. When I first compared the hw differences, it only made a tiny difference, but I guess the more performance squeezing happens the bigger effect small pixel differences make.
fyi #103 is winning a 3rd spot, congrats!

@YassineYousfi it is quite disappointing that you think it is "fair" to deviate from the posted evaluation specifications which clearly state that submissions will be run on a CPU instance unless GPU is required (by the submission). Of course, it is disappointing because disregarding the specifications and inventing new private criteria is the opposite of "fair".

Refer to:
> **_If your inflation script requires a GPU, it will run on a T4 GPU instance (RAM: 26GB, VRAM: 16GB), if it doesn't it will run on a CPU instance (CPU: 4, RAM: 16GB)._**

The purpose of that specification is to remove any ambiguity on what we may privately hold to be "fair" or not.

And while I appreciate the congratulations -- #103 is probably in **2nd** place with Comma's official scoring applied across the board.

To re-iterate, the choice was between:

(i) run on different hw - making the scores not comparable between submissions, because they're not computed with the same ground truth video
(ii) run on the same hw - making the score comparable

I chose (ii) which degraded a bunch of submissions, the top 3 submissions were already very close, so there was a shake-up. 

Would you like to renounce your 3rd place?

@YassineYousfi

Could you help me understand (i)? If all scores are being compared based on the original scoring criteria and hardware options, _which were made available to all competitors_, in what way do they become not comparable? Anyone could have selected and optimized for either hardware configuration, making the playing field level. Switching some competitors to different hardware than their selected option makes the scores _not comparable_, as some competitors are being scored with their preferred selection and some are being scored with not-their-selection that they may not have optimized for, in a way that affects different strategies by different amounts.

But, to re-iterate my point, if you want to be fair, this was never a choice for you to make _after_ the submission deadline.

> Would you like to renounce your 3rd place?

What makes you ask that? My preference would be that all submissions are scored in accordance with the originally posted rules that competitors were building their submissions for, and whatever way that impacts the leaderboards stands as the final results. If you want to be extra charitable, you could even score both CPU/GPU and keep the best. That way everyone gets scored at least in accordance to their own selection, and if one is favored, folks who missed it get an opportunity to benefit.

With that being said, I am perfectly comfortable with @AaronLeslie138 receiving my prize since all the top solutions were derived from his breakthrough.

re: renouncing your 3rd place.

I'm asking that because it seems that you're not willing to have a productive discussion about the evaluation score in the open :) I'm happy to be proven wrong, or re-evaluate my trade-offs, but trying to influence things privately is not the way to do so :) 

If you read the scores as a black box number, then I agree that each solution gets to pick the runtime and optimizes w.r.t. that runtime and gets scored. But the score has a physical meaning that depends on the ground truth video, so having that be mismatched makes things non comparable 100%. One way to fix this is to make the score relative to a baseline computed on the solution runtime. Maybe for the next phase, or maybe we'll just do one runtime.

re: breakthrough open solutions.
